d: Every question asks for an expectation or a probability. What changes is the tool that gets you there without brute force:

$$\begin{array}{ll} \textsf{Section} & \textsf{Tool and the question it answers} \\ \hline \textsf{Optimal stopping} & \textsf{first-step analysis, Bellman: when to stop a game you may stop any time} \\ \textsf{Distributions} & \textsf{normal, order statistics, counting, Poisson process: how big, how long} \\ \textsf{Patterns \& walks} & \textsf{states, martingales, indicators: waiting times, which barrier first} \\ \textsf{Bayes \& estimation} & \textsf{likelihood, prior, odds: what the data say about a parameter} \\ \textsf{Dependence} & \textsf{covariance, conditional expectation: what one variable says about another} \\ \textsf{Returns \& LLN} & \textsf{sums, Jensen, LLN: what an average can and cannot tell you} \\ \textsf{Edge \& sizing} & \textsf{Kelly: with a positive edge, how much to bet} \end{array}$$
Each item: what it answers → definition → symbols → worked example with numbers → key points.
Offer stream (stopping, distributions): buyers arrive one by one with independent offers $U_i\sim\mathrm{Unif}(0,1)$; seeing another offer costs $c=0.01$. It is #1's 100-sided die divided by 100.
Signal Q (counting, estimation, Bayes): a signal calls the market's daily direction, right with unknown probability $p$, days independent; over 20 days it was right 12 times, wrong 8.
Position (walks, Poisson): orders arrive as a Poisson process with rate $\lambda=2$ per minute; each order moves the price $\pm1$ tick with probability 1/2. Take-profit at $+3$, stop-loss at $-2$.
Strategy S (returns, LLN, Kelly): daily return with mean $\mu=0.04\%$, sd $\sigma=1\%$, $T=252$ days a year, days independent.
Answers: in the offer stream, how many offers until a "good" one?
Expectation: $E(X)=\sum_jx_jP(X=x_j)$ or $\int xf(x)\,dx$. Linearity $E(X+Y)=E(X)+E(Y)$ holds with no independence.

Geometric: independent trials with success probability $p$, $q=1-p$. Failures before the first success $X\sim\mathrm{Geom}(p)$: $P(X=k)=q^kp$, $E(X)=q/p$. Total trials $Y=X+1\sim\mathrm{FS}(p)$: $E(Y)=1/p$.
First-step analysis (law of total expectation, conditioning on the first trial): if a failure puts you back at the start, $$E(X)=0\cdot p+\big(1+E(X)\big)q\ \Rightarrow\ E(X)=\frac qp$$
Example (offers): "good" = $U>0.9$, $p=0.1$: 10 offers on average, 9 of them rejected.
Key point: in #1 under "stop at $\ge k$", the paid rerolls are $\mathrm{Geom}(p)$ with mean $1/p-1$. #1's Bellman equation and #3's HH equations are both first-step analysis.
Answers: with a limited number of tries, when do you stop?

DP: $J_N(x)=g_N(x)$, $J_k(x)=\max_u E\{g_k+J_{k+1}(\text{next state})\}$. $J_k$ = value of being at stage $k$ in state $x$, playing optimally from then on. The tail of an optimal policy is optimal (principle of optimality).
Example: 6-sided die, at most 3 rolls, take the value when you stop.

$$\begin{array}{llll} \textsf{Roll} & \textsf{value of continuing} & \textsf{rule} & \textsf{value here} \\ \hline \textsf{3} & \textsf{-} & \textsf{must take} & \textsf{3.5} \\ \textsf{2} & \textsf{3.5} & \textsf{stop at} \ge4 & \tfrac36(3.5)+\tfrac16(4+5+6)=4.25 \\ \textsf{1} & \textsf{4.25} & \textsf{stop at} \ge5 & \tfrac46(4.25)+\tfrac16(5+6)=14/3 \end{array}$$
Relationship: more rolls left → higher value of continuing → higher threshold.
Answers: unlimited tries, each costs $c$. When do you accept?
The situation after a reroll equals the start, so the value is one number $V$: $$V=E\big[\max(X,\,V-c)\big]$$ $X$ = this roll or offer; $V-c$ = value of continuing.
Consequence 1: $V-c$ is constant, so stop iff $X\ge m$ with $m=V-c$ (a threshold).
Consequence 2: subtract $m$ from both sides: $$c=E\big[(X-m)^+\big]$$ At the threshold, the expected improvement from one more look equals its cost.

Example (offers, $c=0.01$): $E[(U-m)^+]=\int_m^1(u-m)\,du=\frac{(1-m)^2}{2}=0.01$, so $m=1-\sqrt{0.02}=0.859$, $V=0.869$. Check: accept with probability 0.141, so 7.07 offers seen; accepted mean $(1+m)/2=0.929$; $0.929-0.01\times6.07=0.869$.

$$\begin{array}{lc} \textsf{Policy} & \textsf{expected net payoff} \\ \hline \textsf{fix } n=9 \textsf{ in advance, take the best: } \tfrac{9}{10}-0.08 & \textsf{0.820} \\ \textsf{decide as you go, stop at} \ge0.859 & \textsf{0.869} \end{array}$$
Discrete version (#1, $N=100$, $c=1$): $\frac{(N-m)(N-m+1)}{2N}=c$ gives $m=86.35$, threshold 87, $V=87.36$; $N-m\approx\sqrt{2Nc}$.
Answers: two buyers score your item with normal, possibly correlated scores. How likely is A's score higher?
$X=\mu+\sigma Z$ with $Z\sim N(0,1)$ is $N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ (the second parameter is the variance). Independent normals add: means add, variances add.
$\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)=E[(X-EX)(Y-EY)]$, $\mathrm{Corr}=\mathrm{Cov}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Var}X\,\mathrm{Var}Y}\in[-1,1]$, and $$\mathrm{Var}(X-Y)=\mathrm{Var}X+\mathrm{Var}Y-2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$$
Multivariate normal: every linear combination $t_1X_1+\dots+t_kX_k$ is normal. Each $X_j$ normal on its own is not enough.
Example (scores, sd 1, A higher by 0.5 on average): $P(X>Y)=\Phi(0.5/\mathrm{SD}(X-Y))$.

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \rho & \mathrm{SD}(X-Y) & P(X>Y) \\ \hline \textsf{0} & \textsf{1.414} & \textsf{0.638} \\ \textsf{0.5} & \textsf{1.000} & \textsf{0.691} \\ \textsf{0.9} & \textsf{0.447} & \textsf{0.868} \end{array}$$ With equal means the answer is 1/2 for every $\rho<1$: correlation changes the scale of $X-Y$, not its centre.
Counterexample: $Y=SX$ with a random sign $S$. $Y\sim N(0,1)$ but $(X,Y)$ is not jointly normal; $P(X>Y)=P(S=-1)P(X>0)=1/4$ and $P(X=Y)=1/2$.
Answers: after $n$ offers, how high is the best one on average?
$F(x)=P(X\le x)$; survival $P(X>x)=1-F(x)$. For $X\ge0$: $$E(X)=\int_0^\infty P(X>x)\,dx$$
Order statistics $X_{(1)}\le\dots\le X_{(n)}$. "The $j$-th smallest $\le x$" = "at least $j$ of them $\le x$", so for i.i.d. $X_i$: $P(X_{(n)}\le x)=F(x)^n$, $P(X_{(1)}>x)=(1-F(x))^n$.
Uniform case: $U_{(j)}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(j,\,n-j+1)$, mean $\frac{j}{n+1}$. Max: $\int_0^1(1-x^n)dx=\frac{n}{n+1}$; min: $\frac{1}{n+1}$.

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} \textsf{n} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{2} & \textsf{5} & \textsf{10} & \textsf{20} \\ \hline E(\textsf{best offer}) & \textsf{0.500} & \textsf{0.667} & \textsf{0.833} & \textsf{0.909} & \textsf{0.952} \end{array}$$ The marginal gain $\frac{1}{(n+1)(n+2)}$ shrinks, which is why paid search must stop.
Key point: the best of $n$ zero-alpha backtests looks better as $n$ grows: selection bias.
Answers: when does the first ace (or first crash) arrive?

Naive probability: with equally likely outcomes, $P(A)=\frac{\#\text{favourable}}{\#\text{total}}$. Choose a sample space where outcomes really are equally likely: here, the set of positions of the 4 aces, $\binom{52}{4}$ sets.
First ace at $k$: position $k$ is an ace, the other 3 are among the $52-k$ later ones: $$P(k)=\frac{\binom{52-k}{3}}{\binom{52}{4}},\quad k=1,\dots,49$$
Indicator trick (fundamental bridge $E(I_A)=P(A)$): $I_j=1$ if non-ace $j$ precedes all 4 aces, probability 1/5. $E(\text{non-aces before first ace})=48/5=9.6$, position 10.6.
Example (Q-style): 4 crash weeks among 52, placed at random. Expected week of the first crash 10.6; $P(\text{first within 10 weeks})=1-\binom{42}{4}/\binom{52}{4}=0.587$.
Key point: with replacement the wait is geometric with mean 13; without replacement it is shorter because the share of aces rises.
Answers: orders arrive at random. How long until the next one, or the $k$-th?
Poisson process with rate $\lambda$: arrivals in a window of length $t$ are $\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda t)$; disjoint windows independent. $N_t$ = count in $[0,t]$, $T_k$ = time of the $k$-th arrival.

Count-time duality: $P(T_1>t)=P(N_t=0)=e^{-\lambda t}$, so $T_1\sim\mathrm{Expo}(\lambda)$, mean $1/\lambda$. Gaps are i.i.d. Expo, so $T_k\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(k,\lambda)$, mean $k/\lambda$, variance $k/\lambda^2$, and $P(T_k>t)=P(N_t<k)$.
Memoryless: $P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=P(T>t)$.
Example (position, $\lambda=2$/min): the 3rd order arrives after 1.5 minutes on average; $P(T_3>1)=P(N_1<3)=e^{-2}(1+2+2)=0.677$.
Inspection paradox: arriving at a random time, the gap you land in has mean $2/\lambda$, not $1/\lambda$ (long gaps are more likely to be hit).
Answers: how many offers until two in a row above 0.5? Call "above 0.5" H: it is waiting for HH with a fair coin.
States = longest matched prefix. HH: $e_0=1+\tfrac12e_1+\tfrac12e_0$, $e_1=1+\tfrac12e_0$ ⇒ $e_1=4$, $e_0=6$. HT: after H another H keeps progress, so 2 + 2 = 4.
General formula (a gambler arrives before each toss, bets on the pattern at fair odds; total net winnings is a martingale): $$E[T_A]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}2^k\,\mathbf 1\{A_{1:k}=A_{n-k+1:n}\}$$

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \textsf{Pattern} & k \textsf{ with prefix = suffix} & E[T_A] \\ \hline \textsf{HT} & \textsf{2} & \textsf{4} \\ \textsf{HH} & \textsf{1,2} & \textsf{6} \\ \textsf{THH} & \textsf{3} & \textsf{8} \\ \textsf{HHH} & \textsf{1,2,3} & \textsf{14} \\ \textsf{HHTTHH} & \textsf{1,2,6} & \textsf{70} \end{array}$$
Key points: the difference is not the probability (HH and HT each 1/4 in two tosses) but whether progress survives a failure. "Which comes first, HH or HT" is a race: 1/2 each.
Answers: the position exits at $+3$ or $-2$. Which first, and after how many orders?
Martingale: $E|Z_n|<\infty$ and $E[Z_{n+1}\mid Z_n,\dots,Z_1]=Z_n$. The symmetric walk $S_n$ is one. Stopping time $\tau$: whether you have stopped by $n$ depends only on the path up to $n$.

Optional stopping: $E[S_\tau]=S_0$ if $\tau<\infty$ with $E\tau<\infty$ and the stopped walk is bounded. Then $aP-b(1-P)=0$: $$P(+a\text{ first})=\frac{b}{a+b},\qquad E[\tau]=ab\ \ (\text{via the martingale } S_n^2-n)$$
Example (position, $a=3$, $b=2$): take-profit probability $2/5=0.4$; $3\times2=6$ orders; at 2 orders a minute, 3 minutes.
Counterexample: no lower barrier, stop at the first $+1$: $E[S_\tau]=1\ne0$, because $E\tau=\infty$ and the walk is unbounded below. Stating the conditions matters.
Up with probability $p$, down $q=1-p$. $S_n$ is no longer a martingale; $Z_n=(q/p)^{S_n}$ is: $E[(q/p)^X]=p\frac qp+q\frac pq=1$.
$$P(+a\text{ first})=\frac{1-(q/p)^{b}}{1-(q/p)^{a+b}},\qquad E\tau=\frac{aP-b(1-P)}{p-q}\ \ (\text{Wald})$$

$$\begin{array}{lcccc} a=b & \textsf{p} & P(+a\textsf{ first}) & E\tau \\ \hline \textsf{10} & \textsf{0.50} & \textsf{0.500} & \textsf{100} \\ \textsf{10} & \textsf{0.51} & \textsf{0.599} & \textsf{98.7} \\ \textsf{10} & \textsf{0.55} & \textsf{0.882} & \textsf{76.3} \\ \textsf{50} & \textsf{0.51} & \textsf{0.881} & \textsf{1904} \end{array}$$
Example (position with $p=0.51$): take-profit probability 0.424 instead of 0.4.
Relationship: a tiny edge matters little over short distances and a lot over long ones.
Answers: in a random permutation, how many items stay in place?
$X=\sum_jI_j$ with $E(I_j)=1/n$, so $E(X)=1$ for every $n$; the $I_j$ are dependent but linearity does not care.
Variance: $\mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_j)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}-\frac1{n^2}=\frac{1}{n^2(n-1)}$, so $\mathrm{Var}(X)=(1-\tfrac1n)+\tfrac1n=1$.
Poisson paradigm: the count of many rare, weakly dependent events is about $\mathrm{Pois}(\lambda)$ with $\lambda=\sum p_j$.

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} \textsf{k} & \textsf{0} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{2} & \textsf{3} & \textsf{4} \\ \hline n=10 \textsf{ (simulated)} & \textsf{0.366} & \textsf{0.369} & \textsf{0.184} & \textsf{0.061} & \textsf{0.016} \\ \mathrm{Pois}(1) & \textsf{0.368} & \textsf{0.368} & \textsf{0.184} & \textsf{0.061} & \textsf{0.015} \end{array}$$ $P(\text{no fixed point})\to1/e=0.368$.
Answers: from the data alone, what is signal Q's hit rate?
Likelihood: the probability of the observed data as a function of the parameter. $h$ hits, $t$ misses: $$L(p)=p^h(1-p)^t,\qquad \ell'(p)=\frac hp-\frac{t}{1-p}=0\ \Rightarrow\ \hat p=\frac{h}{h+t}$$
Example (Q): 12 right, 8 wrong: $\hat p=0.6$. With 3 right, 0 wrong: $\hat p=1$, "never wrong". With little data the MLE goes to extremes.

Posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. Prior $p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ (density $\propto p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}$; read $a-1$, $b-1$ as hits and misses already seen): $$p^h(1-p)^t\cdot p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{Beta}(a+h,\,b+t)$$ Conjugacy: recognise the shape, no integral needed.
Posterior mean as a weighted average: $$\frac{a+h}{a+b+n}=w\,\frac hn+(1-w)\frac{a}{a+b},\qquad w=\frac{n}{a+b+n}$$ MAP $=\frac{a+h-1}{a+b+n-2}$ (equals the MLE under the uniform prior).

$$\begin{array}{llccc} \textsf{Prior} & \textsf{meaning} & \textsf{posterior} & \textsf{mean} & \textsf{95\% interval} \\ \hline \mathrm{Beta}(1,1) & \textsf{knows nothing} & \mathrm{Beta}(13,9) & \textsf{0.591} & (0.38,\,0.78) \\ \mathrm{Beta}(10,10) & \textsf{18 days seen, half right} & \mathrm{Beta}(22,18) & \textsf{0.550} & (0.40,\,0.70) \\ \textsf{none} & \textsf{MLE} & \textsf{-} & \textsf{0.600} & \textsf{-} \end{array}$$
Key point: short-history hit rates, ICs and Sharpe ratios should be shrunk toward a sensible prior; with much data $w\to1$ and the approaches agree.
Answers: is Q a real signal (right 55% of days) or noise (50%)?

Odds form: $$\frac{P(A\mid D)}{P(B\mid D)}=\frac{P(A)}{P(B)}\cdot\frac{P(D\mid A)}{P(D\mid B)}$$ The likelihood is a product only because days are independent given which hypothesis is true (conditional independence). Unconditionally they are not.
In logs each day adds a term: a right day $\log(0.55/0.5)=+0.0953$, a wrong day $\log(0.45/0.5)=-0.1054$. Updating day by day equals updating once with all data.

$$\begin{array}{lcc} \textsf{Right / wrong} & \textsf{log LR} & P(\textsf{real}\mid D) \\ \hline 12/8 & \textsf{0.301} & \textsf{0.575} \\ 60/40 & \textsf{1.504} & \textsf{0.818} \\ 550/450 & \textsf{5.008} & \textsf{0.993} \end{array}$$ If Q is real the log LR grows only 0.005 a day: about $\log19/0.005\approx590$ days to reach 95%.
Several coins per box: "redraw each flip" gives the mixture probability per flip; "draw once and keep" gives a mixture of products. Ask which.
Answers: 10 heads in a row. Is the coin fair?
p-value $=P(\text{data this extreme}\mid H_0)=2^{-10}\approx0.001$ (one-sided): reject at usual levels. It is not $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$, which needs a prior and an alternative.
Prior: fair with probability $\pi$, otherwise two-headed: $$P(\text{fair}\mid D)=\frac{\pi\,2^{-10}}{\pi\,2^{-10}+(1-\pi)}$$
$$\begin{array}{lc} \pi & P(\textsf{fair}\mid 10\textsf{ heads}) \\ \hline \textsf{0.99} & \textsf{0.088} \\ \textsf{0.999} & \textsf{0.494} \end{array}$$

Key points: how was the coin found (picked from many for its streak = multiple testing)? Was $n=10$ fixed, or did someone stop at the streak? The p-value depends on the stopping rule; the Bayesian posterior, which uses only the likelihood, does not.
Answers: Q's IC is 0. Does Q tell you nothing?
Independent ⇒ $\mathrm{Cov}=0$, not conversely: covariance measures only linear dependence. $X\sim N(0,1)$, $Y=X^2$: $\mathrm{Cov}=E(X^3)=0$, yet $Y$ is a function of $X$.
Converse holds for jointly normal vectors (zero covariance ⇒ the density factors) and for two 0/1 variables.
Example: signal $s\sim N(0,1)$, return $r=0.1(s^2-1)+\varepsilon$.

$$\begin{array}{lc} \textsf{Quantity} & \textsf{Value} \\ \hline \mathrm{Corr}(s,r)\ (\textsf{IC}) & \textsf{-0.0004} \\ \textsf{mean return, top 10\% of } s & \textsf{0.228} \\ \textsf{mean return, bottom 10\% of } s & \textsf{0.224} \\ \textsf{mean return, middle 80\%} & \textsf{-0.054} \\ \mathrm{Corr}(s^2,r) & \textsf{0.14} \end{array}$$
Key point: check quantile returns, $|s|$ or $s^2$, ranks, mutual information before calling a signal empty.
Answers: given a total, what is one part expected to be?
Symmetry: $X,Y$ i.i.d., $S=X+Y$: $E(X\mid S)=E(Y\mid S)$ and they sum to $S$, so $E(X\mid S)=S/2$. Only i.i.d. is used.
Jointly normal, unequal variances: $$E(X\mid S=s)=\mu_X+\frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}(s-\mu_X-\mu_Y)$$ The surprise is split in proportion to the variances.
Example (position): after two orders the price is up 2 (both moves up), so the first move's expectation is $+1=s/2$.
Example (signal extraction): return = alpha (sd 1%) + noise (sd 4%); a 10% return implies expected alpha $10\%/17=0.59\%$.

items.t: Mean and variance of a sum
d: Answers: how do Strategy S's mean and risk scale from a day to a year?
$E(\sum r_t)=\sum E(r_t)$ always. $\mathrm{Var}(\sum r_t)=\sum\mathrm{Var}(r_t)+2\sum_{s<t}\mathrm{Cov}(r_s,r_t)$; independence removes the covariances.
Example (S, independent): annual mean $252\times0.04\%=10.08\%$, vol $1\%\sqrt{252}=15.87\%$.
With autocorrelation $\rho_k$: $$\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_{t=1}^Tr_t\Big)=T\sigma^2+2\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}(T-k)\rho_k$$ S with AR(1), $\rho=0.1$: annual vol 17.54% instead of 15.87%.
Key point: $\sqrt{252}$ annualisation assumes no autocorrelation; momentum-like dependence understates long-horizon risk.
Simple $R_t=P_t/P_{t-1}-1$; log $r_t=\log(1+R_t)$. Multi-period: $1+R_{0,T}=\prod(1+R_t)$, while log returns add: $r_{0,T}=\sum r_t$.
Example (S): exact compounded mean $(1.0004)^{252}-1=10.60\%$ vs arithmetic sum 10.08%: summing simple returns is an approximation.
Convex $g$ ($g''\ge0$): $E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X])$; concave reverses; equality iff $g$ is linear on the support of $X$ (or $X$ constant).
Options: payoff $(S_T-K)^+$ is convex, so uncertainty adds value (time value).
Compounding: $\log$ is concave, $E[\log(1+R)]<\log(1+E[R])$. Daily log growth $\approx\mu-\sigma^2/2$.

Example (S): per day $0.0004-0.0001/2=0.00035$, so a typical path compounds at $e^{252\times0.00035}-1=9.22\%$, below the 10.60% mean. Annual 10% mean with 30% vol: $10\%-4.5\%=5.5\%$ (volatility drag).
Answers: when can a sample mean be trusted?
Chebyshev: $P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{n\varepsilon^2}$. LLN: for i.i.d. data with finite variance, $\bar X_n\to\mu$ in probability.
Example (S): for $t=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt n=2$, $n=(2\sigma/\mu)^2=2500$ days ≈ 9.9 years. Even then Chebyshev with $\varepsilon=\mu$ only bounds $P(|\bar X-\mu|\ge\mu)$ by 0.25.

What the LLN does not say: it needs a fixed $\mu$ (regimes move it), a large $n$ (the edge is tiny relative to noise), and an unselected sample (the best of many backtests is biased up). It says nothing about costs, capacity or crowding.
Answers: the game pays $+2$ with probability 0.4, $-1$ with 0.6 (EV $+0.2$). What fraction $f$ of capital to bet each round?
Maximise long-run growth $g(f)=E\log(1+fX)$. Win $b$ times the stake with probability $p$: $$g(f)=p\log(1+bf)+q\log(1-f),\qquad f^*=\frac{bp-q}{b}=\frac{\text{edge}}{\text{odds}}$$

$$\begin{array}{lccc} \textsf{f} & \textsf{0.05} & \textsf{0.10} & \textsf{0.20} \\ \hline g(f) \textsf{ per round} & \textsf{0.0074} & \textsf{0.0097} & \textsf{0.0007} \end{array}$$ Half Kelly keeps 76% of the growth; double Kelly keeps almost none. Betting everything is ruin with probability 1.
Normal approximation $f^*=m/s^2=0.2/2.16=0.093$: 7% off, because the payoff is skewed.
Returns with mean $m$ and sd $s$: $g(f)\approx fm-\tfrac12f^2s^2$, so $$f^*=\frac{m}{s^2},\qquad g(f^*)=\frac{m^2}{2s^2}=\frac{SR^2}{2}$$ Several strategies: $F^*=C^{-1}M$.
Example (S): $f^*=0.0004/0.0001=4$× leverage. Annual growth $252(fm-s^2f^2/2)$:

$$\begin{array}{lccccc} \textsf{f} & \textsf{1} & \textsf{2} & \textsf{4} & \textsf{6} & \textsf{8} \\ \hline \textsf{g} & \textsf{8.8\%} & \textsf{15.1\%} & \textsf{20.2\%} & \textsf{15.1\%} & \textsf{0} \end{array}$$

Relationship: $g$ is a parabola symmetric about $f^*$; half Kelly keeps 3/4 of the growth at half the vol; double Kelly earns nothing. Full Kelly halves wealth at some point with probability 1/2. Since $m$ is estimated, practitioners bet a fraction.
Geom($p$) counts failures (mean $q/p$); First Success counts trials including the success (mean $1/p$). Differ by 1.
$N(\mu,\sigma^2)$: second parameter is the variance. $\mathrm{Gamma}(k,\lambda)$ here uses rate $\lambda$ (mean $k/\lambda$); some books use scale $\theta=1/\lambda$.
Correlation coefficient vs AR(1) coefficient vs autocorrelation at lag $k$: say which.

cards.q: A fair 100-sided die shows $1,\dots,100$. After each roll you may stop and take the face value, or pay 1 point and roll again, with no limit on rolls. (1) Define the value $V$ and write the Bellman equation. (2) Why is the optimal policy a threshold, and what is the rule in terms of $V$? (3) Under the policy "stop at $k$ or above", write the expected payoff $f(k)$. (4) Give the optimal $k$ and $V$.
pts: (1) $V$ = expected payoff just before a roll, playing optimally. After seeing $x$: stopping gives $x$; rerolling puts you back in the same situation minus the fee, $V-1$. $$V = E\big[\max(X,\,V-1)\big]$$
(2) $V-1$ is a constant, so stop iff $x \ge V-1$: keep high faces, reroll low ones.

(3) Stop probability per roll $p=\frac{101-k}{100}$; the accepted face is uniform on $\{k,\dots,100\}$ with mean $\frac{k+100}{2}$; the number of rolls is geometric with mean $1/p$, so paid rerolls average $1/p-1$. $$f(k)=\frac{k+100}{2}-\Big(\frac{100}{101-k}-1\Big)$$
cards.pit: The threshold is $V-1$, not $V$; and maximising the average accepted face alone ignores the fees.

cards.q: Same game with an $N$-sided die and reroll cost $c$. Let $m=V-c$ be the continuation value. (1) Derive the indifference condition at $m$. (2) Solve it for the uniform die and give the approximate gap $N-m$. (3) For $N=100$, how does the optimal threshold move for $c=0.5,\,2,\,5$? (4) What changes if you may roll at most $n$ times?
pts: (1) Subtract $m$ from both sides of $V=E[\max(X,m)]$: $$c = E\big[(X-m)^+\big]$$ At the threshold the expected gain from one more roll equals its cost.
(2) $$E[(X-m)^+]=\frac{(N-m)(N-m+1)}{2N}=c \;\Rightarrow\; N-m\approx\sqrt{2Nc}$$ $N=100,\ c=1$: $m\approx 86.35$, $V\approx 87.35$.
(3) $c=0.5 \to k^*=91$; $c=1 \to 87$; $c=2 \to 81$; $c=5 \to 69$. Higher cost, lower threshold; the gap grows like $\sqrt{c}$.

(4) The state must include rolls left; solve by backward induction from the last roll, and the threshold falls as rolls run out. 6-sided die, 3 rolls: last roll worth 3.5; second roll stop at $\ge 4$ (worth 4.25); first roll stop at $\ge 5$ (worth $14/3$).

cards.q: $X, Y$ are standard normal. (1) Find $P(X>Y)$ when they are independent. (2) What if they are jointly normal with correlation $\rho<1$? (3) What happens at $\rho=1$? (4) If instead $\mu_X-\mu_Y=0.5$ with unit variances, how does $\rho$ change $P(X>Y)$? (5) What assumption does the correlated case need?
pts: (1) $D=X-Y\sim N(0,2)$: continuous and symmetric about 0, so $P(D>0)=1/2$.
(2) $\mathrm{Var}(D)=1+1-2\rho=2-2\rho>0$ and the mean is still 0, so still $1/2$. Correlation changes the scale of $D$, not its centre.
(3) $X=Y$ almost surely, $D=0$: $P(X>Y)=0$ and $P(X\ge Y)=1$.

(4) $$P(X>Y)=\Phi\Big(\frac{\mu_X-\mu_Y}{\sqrt{2-2\rho}}\Big)$$ $\rho=0$: 0.638; $\rho=0.5$: 0.691; $\rho=0.9$: 0.868. High correlation shrinks the noise in the difference, so the mean gap shows through.
(5) Joint normality. Normal marginals alone do not make $X-Y$ normal.

cards.q: $U_1,\dots,U_n$ are i.i.d. $U(0,1)$ and $M=\max_i U_i$. (1) Find the CDF of $M$. (2) Find $E[M]$, and give the value for $n=2$. (3) Find $E[\min_i U_i]$. (4) Give $E[U_{(j)}]$ for the $j$-th smallest and the intuition.
pts: (1) $M\le x$ iff every $U_i\le x$; by independence $P(M\le x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$.
(2) Integrate the tail: $$E[M]=\int_0^1(1-x^n)\,dx=\frac{n}{n+1}$$ (or use the density $nx^{n-1}$). $n=2$: $2/3$.
(4) $U_{(j)}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(j,\,n-j+1)$ with mean $\frac{j}{n+1}$: the $n$ points cut $[0,1]$ into $n+1$ gaps of equal expected length.
cards.pit: Selection bias is the same effect: the best of $n$ zero-skill backtests looks better as $n$ grows.

cards.q: A shuffled 52-card deck contains 4 aces; cards are drawn without replacement. (1) Find $P(\text{first ace on draw }k)$ and its support. (2) Check $k=1$. (3) Find the expected position of the first ace using indicators. (4) Compare with drawing with replacement.
pts: (1) Only the 4 ace positions matter, and all $\binom{52}{4}$ sets are equally likely. Position $k$ is an ace and the other 3 are among the $52-k$ later positions: $$P=\frac{\binom{52-k}{3}}{\binom{52}{4}},\qquad k=1,\dots,49$$
(2) $\binom{51}{3}/\binom{52}{4}=4/52=0.0769$, the chance the top card is an ace.

(3) $I_j=1$ if non-ace $j$ comes before all 4 aces; its 5 relative orders are equally likely, so $P(I_j=1)=1/5$. Expected non-aces before the first ace $=48/5=9.6$, position $=10.6$. Linearity needs no independence.
(4) With replacement the wait is geometric with $p=1/13$, mean 13. Without replacement it is shorter: the share of aces rises as non-aces are used up.

cards.q: Arrivals follow a Poisson process with rate $\lambda$: $N_t$ = number of arrivals in $[0,t]$, $T_k$ = time of the $k$-th arrival. (1) Derive the distribution of $T_1$. (2) Give the distribution, mean and variance of $T_k$. (3) State the memoryless property. (4) What is the inspection paradox?
pts: (1) Count-time duality: $P(T_1>t)=P(N_t=0)=e^{-\lambda t}$, so $T_1\sim\mathrm{Expo}(\lambda)$, mean $1/\lambda$.

(2) Interarrival times are i.i.d. $\mathrm{Expo}(\lambda)$ (independent increments), so $T_k\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(k,\lambda)$: mean $k/\lambda$, variance $k/\lambda^2$. Equivalently $P(T_k>t)=P(N_t<k)$, a Poisson tail.
(3) $P(T>s+t\mid T>s)=P(T>t)$: time already waited does not change the remaining wait.
(4) Show up at a random time: the gap you land in has mean $2/\lambda$, not $1/\lambda$, because long gaps are more likely to be hit.

cards.q: A fair coin is tossed until HH appears. (1) Define the states. (2) Write the first-step equations. (3) Solve for the expected number of tosses. (4) Why is the answer for HT only 4?
pts: (1) State = how much of HH the latest tosses match: 0 (start or last toss T), 1 (last toss H), 2 (done). $e_i$ = expected remaining tosses, $e_2=0$.
(2) $$e_0=1+\tfrac12 e_1+\tfrac12 e_0,\qquad e_1=1+\tfrac12\cdot 0+\tfrac12 e_0$$
(3) The first gives $e_0=2+e_1$; substituting, $e_1=2+\tfrac12 e_1$, so $e_1=4$ and $e_0=6$.
(4) For HT a failure after H (another H) keeps the progress: $e_1=1+\tfrac12 e_1=2$, $e_0=4$ (wait for the first H, 2, then for a T, 2). For HH a failure resets to state 0.

cards.q: Fair coin, target pattern $A$ of length $n$. (1) Give the formula for the expected waiting time. (2) Apply it to HHH, THH and HHTTHH. (3) Which appears first, HH or HT, and why is that a different question from (1)?
pts: (1) Gamblers martingale (a new gambler bets on $A$ before each toss): $$E[T_A]=\sum_{k=1}^{n}2^{k}\,\mathbf 1\{\text{first }k\text{ letters of }A=\text{last }k\text{ letters}\}$$
(2) HHH: $k=1,2,3$, $2+4+8=14$. THH: only $k=3$, 8. HHTTHH: $k=1,2,6$, $2+4+64=70$. Self-overlapping patterns take longer.
(3) Probability 1/2 each: after the first H, the next toss decides. The expected waiting times differ (6 vs 4), but "which comes first" is a race, not a waiting time.

cards.q: A symmetric random walk $S_n$ starts at 0 and moves $\pm1$ with probability 1/2. $\tau$ = first time it hits $+a$ or $-b$ ($a,b$ positive integers). (1) Why is $S_n$ a martingale? (2) Use optional stopping to find $P(\text{hit }+a\text{ first})$, stating the conditions. (3) Find $E[\tau]$. (4) Give a case where optional stopping fails.
pts: (2) $\tau$ is finite with $E\tau<\infty$, and $|S_{\tau\wedge n}|\le\max(a,b)$, so $E[S_\tau]=S_0=0$: $aP-b(1-P)=0$, $$P=\frac{b}{a+b}$$
(3) $S_n^2-n$ is also a martingale, so $E[\tau]=E[S_\tau^2]=a^2\frac{b}{a+b}+b^2\frac{a}{a+b}=ab$.
(4) No lower barrier, $\tau$ = first time at $+1$: $S_\tau=1$, so $E[S_\tau]=1\ne0$. Here $E\tau=\infty$ and the walk is unbounded below.

cards.q: Same walk, but it moves up with probability $p\ne\tfrac12$ and down with $q=1-p$; barriers $+a$ and $-b$. (1) Find a martingale to use. (2) Derive $P(\text{hit }+a\text{ first})$. (3) Give the values for $a=b=10$ with $p=0.51$ and $p=0.55$, and for $a=b=50$ with $p=0.51$. (4) How do you get the expected duration?
pts: (1) $Z_n=(q/p)^{S_n}$: $E[(q/p)^{X}]=p\frac qp+q\frac pq=1$, so $E[Z_{n+1}\mid Z_n]=Z_n$.
(2) $E[Z_\tau]=1$: $P(q/p)^a+(1-P)(q/p)^{-b}=1$, so $$P=\frac{1-(q/p)^{b}}{1-(q/p)^{a+b}}$$ (gambler's ruin starting at $b$ out of $a+b$).
(3) $a=b=10$: 0.599 at $p=0.51$, 0.882 at $p=0.55$. $a=b=50$, $p=0.51$: 0.881. A small drift accumulates over distant barriers.
(4) Wald: $E[S_\tau]=(p-q)E[\tau]$, so $E\tau=\dfrac{aP-b(1-P)}{p-q}$.

cards.q: $\sigma$ is a uniformly random permutation of $n$ elements and $X$ is its number of fixed points. (1) Find $E[X]$. (2) Find $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. (3) What is the limiting distribution, and the limit of $P(X=0)$?
pts: (1) $X=\sum_j I_j$, $I_j=\mathbf 1\{\sigma(j)=j\}$, $E[I_j]=1/n$, so $E[X]=1$ for every $n$. The $I_j$ are dependent, but linearity does not care.
(2) $\mathrm{Cov}(I_i,I_j)=\frac{1}{n(n-1)}-\frac1{n^2}=\frac{1}{n^2(n-1)}$. $$\mathrm{Var}(X)=n\cdot\tfrac1n\big(1-\tfrac1n\big)+n(n-1)\cdot\frac{1}{n^2(n-1)}=1\quad(n\ge2)$$
(3) Poisson(1) (many rare, weakly dependent events). $P(X=0)\to 1/e\approx 0.368$, from inclusion-exclusion $P(X\ge1)=1-\frac1{2!}+\frac1{3!}-\cdots$.

cards.q: A coin has unknown head probability $p$; you see $h$ heads and $t$ tails, $n=h+t$. (1) Derive the MLE. (2) With a $\mathrm{Beta}(a,b)$ prior, find the posterior. (3) Write the posterior mean as a weighted average, and give the MAP. (4) Evaluate both approaches for 3 heads, 0 tails with a uniform prior.
pts: (1) $\ell(p)=h\log p+t\log(1-p)$; $\ell'(p)=\frac hp-\frac{t}{1-p}=0$ gives $\hat p=\frac{h}{h+t}$.
(2) Posterior $\propto p^{h}(1-p)^{t}\cdot p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}$, i.e. $\mathrm{Beta}(a+h,\,b+t)$: Beta is conjugate to the Binomial.
(3) $$\tilde p=\frac{a+h}{a+b+n}=w\,\frac hn+(1-w)\frac{a}{a+b},\qquad w=\frac{n}{a+b+n}$$ MAP $=\frac{a+h-1}{a+b+n-2}$; under the uniform prior MAP = MLE.
(4) MLE $=1$ (absurd after 3 tosses); posterior mean $=4/5=0.8$. With lots of data $w\to1$ and the two agree.
cards.pit: Short-history hit rates, ICs and Sharpe ratios need the same shrinkage toward a sensible prior.

cards.q: A box is chosen with prior $P(A)=\pi$. Box A's coin has head probability $p_A$, box B's $p_B$. You see $h$ heads and $t$ tails. (1) What independence assumption gives the likelihood? (2) Write the posterior odds. (3) Why work in logs? (4) Fair coin vs a $3/4$ coin, prior 1/2, three heads: find $P(\text{fair})$. (5) If a box holds several coins, what must you ask?
pts: (1) Given the box, flips are independent: $P(D\mid A)=p_A^h(1-p_A)^t$. Unconditionally they are not (early heads shift belief).
(2) $$\frac{P(A\mid D)}{P(B\mid D)}=\frac{\pi}{1-\pi}\Big(\frac{p_A}{p_B}\Big)^{h}\Big(\frac{1-p_A}{1-p_B}\Big)^{t}$$ posterior odds = prior odds × likelihood ratio.
(3) Each flip adds one term ($\log\frac{p_A}{p_B}$ or $\log\frac{1-p_A}{1-p_B}$), in any order; avoids underflow; the running sum is the SPRT statistic.
(5) Is a coin redrawn each flip (each flip has the mixture probability) or drawn once and kept (likelihood is a mixture of products $\sum_c w_c\,p_c^h(1-p_c)^t$)?

cards.q: A coin claimed to be fair shows 10 heads in a row. (1) Compute the p-value under the fair-coin null. (2) Why is that not the probability the coin is fair? (3) With a prior of 99% fair and 1% two-headed, find $P(\text{fair}\mid\text{data})$; repeat with 99.9%. (4) What would you ask about how the data arose?
pts: (1) One-sided $2^{-10}\approx 0.00098$: reject fairness at any usual level.
(2) The p-value is $P(\text{data}\mid H_0)$. $P(H_0\mid\text{data})$ needs a prior and an alternative.
(4) Was this coin picked out of many because it looked streaky (multiple testing)? Was $n=10$ fixed in advance, or did someone stop at the streak?

cards.q: (1) Does zero correlation imply independence? (2) Give two counterexamples. (3) Under what conditions does it? (4) Give the trap where both variables are normal. (5) What does this mean for signal research?
pts: (1) No. Independence ⇒ zero covariance, not the converse: covariance only measures linear dependence.
(2) $X\sim N(0,1)$, $Y=X^2$: $\mathrm{Cov}=E[X^3]=0$, yet $Y$ is a function of $X$. Discrete: $X$ uniform on $\{-1,0,1\}$, $Y=X^2$.
(3) $(X,Y)$ jointly normal: with $\rho=0$ the joint density factors into the marginals. Also two 0/1 variables.
(4) $Y=SX$ with an independent random sign $S$: both $N(0,1)$, $\mathrm{Cov}=0$, but $|Y|=|X|$. $X+Y=0$ with probability 1/2, so not jointly normal.
(5) An IC near 0 does not mean no relation: returns can be U-shaped in the signal. Check quantile returns, $|s|$ or $s^2$, ranks, mutual information.

cards.q: $X, Y$ are i.i.d. normal and $S=X+Y$. (1) Find $E[X\mid S=s]$ by symmetry. (2) Give a second proof that uses normality. (3) Generalise to independent $X\sim N(\mu_X,\sigma_X^2)$, $Y\sim N(\mu_Y,\sigma_Y^2)$. (4) Apply it: true alpha $\sim N(0,1\%^2)$, noise $\sim N(0,4\%^2)$, observed return 10%.
pts: (1) $(X,S)$ and $(Y,S)$ have the same law, so $E[X\mid S]=E[Y\mid S]$; they sum to $E[S\mid S]=S$, hence $s/2$. Only i.i.d. is used.
(2) $S$ and $D=X-Y$ are jointly normal with $\mathrm{Cov}=\mathrm{Var}X-\mathrm{Var}Y=0$, hence independent: $E[X\mid S]=\tfrac12(S+E[D])=S/2$.
(3) $$E[X\mid S=s]=\mu_X+\frac{\sigma_X^2}{\sigma_X^2+\sigma_Y^2}\,(s-\mu_X-\mu_Y)$$ The surprise is split in proportion to the variances.
(4) Weight $=\frac{1}{1+16}=\frac1{17}$: estimated alpha $=10\%/17=0.59\%$. Noisy observations are shrunk hard.

cards.q: A strategy has a positive sample mean return. (1) What does the law of large numbers actually guarantee, and under what assumptions? (2) Why may there be no fixed mean to converge to? (3) How much data does a 2 bp daily edge with 1% daily vol need for $t=2$? (4) What does selection do to the sample mean? (5) What else does LLN say nothing about?
pts: (1) $\bar X_n\to\mu$ if returns are i.i.d. (or stationary and ergodic) with a fixed $\mu$, as $n\to\infty$.
(2) Non-stationarity: the true mean drifts across regimes.
(3) $t=\frac{\mu}{\sigma}\sqrt n=2 \Rightarrow n=(2\sigma/\mu)^2=(2\cdot100/2)^2=10{,}000$ days, about 40 years.
(4) The strategy was chosen because its sample mean was high, so that mean is biased upward (winner's curse, multiple testing).
(5) Costs, capacity and crowding: a real positive mean can still be eaten after it is traded.

cards.q: (1) State Jensen's inequality and the equality condition. (2) Give an option-pricing example. (3) Give the compounding example, with numbers for a 10% arithmetic mean and 30% vol.
pts: (1) Convex $g$: $E[g(X)]\ge g(E[X])$; concave flips it. Equality iff $g$ is linear on the support of $X$ (e.g. $X$ constant).
(2) The payoff $(S_T-K)^+$ is convex, so uncertainty in $S_T$ adds value: options have time value.
(3) $\log$ is concave: $E[\log(1+R)]<\log(1+E[R])$. Growth $\approx\mu-\sigma^2/2=10\%-4.5\%=5.5\%$ a year (volatility drag).

cards.q: Daily returns $r_t$ are independent with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$. (1) Give the mean, variance and vol of the $T$-day sum. (2) What changes for the compounded return? (3) What if returns are autocorrelated with $\rho_k$? (4) What does this imply for $\sqrt{252}$ annualisation?
pts: (1) Mean $T\mu$ (linearity); variance $T\sigma^2$ (independence removes covariances); vol $\sigma\sqrt T$.
(2) $E\big[\prod(1+r_t)\big]-1=(1+\mu)^T-1\ne T\mu$; only log returns add exactly.
(3) $$\mathrm{Var}\Big(\sum_t r_t\Big)=T\sigma^2+2\sigma^2\sum_{k=1}^{T-1}(T-k)\rho_k$$ Momentum ($\rho>0$) makes long-horizon risk larger than $\sigma\sqrt T$, mean reversion smaller.
(4) Scaling a daily Sharpe by $\sqrt{252}$ assumes no autocorrelation.

cards.q: A game pays $+2$ with probability 0.4 and $-1$ with probability 0.6 per unit staked. (1) Compute the expected value and standard deviation. (2) Should you stake all your capital each round? (3) What information beyond EV matters?
pts: (2) No: one loss wipes you out, and over many rounds a loss is certain (ruin with probability 1). Playing and sizing are separate decisions.
(3) Capital and ruin constraints, number of rounds, independence across rounds, how reliable 0.4 is, drawdown limits, your utility.

cards.q: Same game: you stake a fraction $f$ of capital each round. (1) Write the long-run growth rate $g(f)$. (2) Find the Kelly fraction. (3) Give $g$ at $f^*$ and at $2f^*$. (4) Why bet less in practice?
pts: (1) $g(f)=0.4\log(1+2f)+0.6\log(1-f)$, the expected log growth per round.
(3) $g(0.1)\approx0.0097$ per round; $g(0.2)\approx0.0007$, essentially zero: over-betting by 2× kills the growth.
(4) $p$ is estimated, and the growth curve falls steeply right of $f^*$; full Kelly has brutal drawdowns. Half Kelly ($f=0.05$) keeps about 76% of the growth.
